planting.note: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 3–4 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; serrated jack-in-the-pulpit is variable in size and color across its native range, so choose nursery stock selected for reliable garden performance.

directions: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 3–4 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; serrated jack-in-the-pulpit is variable in size and color across its native range, so choose nursery stock selected for reliable garden performance. Arisaema serratum is a widespread Japanese woodland aroid with divided, sharply toothed leaflets and a striking hooded flower (spathe) that ranges from green with white stripes to deep purple-black depending on the form, appearing in mid-spring before the compound leaves fully unfurl, followed by a spike of bright red-orange berries in fall. Its variability in size and coloration make different named forms collectible for a shaded woodland garden, where it associates well with hosta, ferns, and other Arisaema species for a layered, textural planting. As with other Arisaema, the plant contains calcium oxalate crystals that irritate skin and mouth if handled or chewed, so keep the attractive berries away from curious pets or children.

planting.note: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 4–5 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; whipcord jack-in-the-pulpit is one of the tallest and most vigorous Arisaema species and benefits from a sheltered site out of strong wind.

directions: Plant dormant tubers in fall, 4–5 inches deep, in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; whipcord jack-in-the-pulpit is one of the tallest and most vigorous Arisaema species and benefits from a sheltered site out of strong wind. Arisaema tortuosum is a dramatic Himalayan species with a tall, mottled false stem supporting a whorl of large, divided leaflets and an upright green hooded flower topped by a long, twisted, whip-like appendage that curls distinctively above the foliage, blooming in early summer. Its imposing height and unusual, contorted flower spike make it one of the most architectural Arisaema species for a shaded border or woodland garden, standing well above the low mounding perennials typically grown nearby. It multiplies steadily by offsets from the tuber and self-sows modestly in favorable conditions, and, like other Arisaema, contains irritating calcium oxalate crystals that make all parts unpleasant to handle or ingest.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; David's epimedium stays evergreen in mild winters and its bright yellow flowers show up especially well against the glossy, dark green, spiny-edged foliage.

directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; David's epimedium stays evergreen in mild winters and its bright yellow flowers show up especially well against the glossy, dark green, spiny-edged foliage. Epimedium davidii is a west-central Chinese species forming a low, evergreen clump of glossy, leathery, spine-toothed leaflets, with wiry stems carrying loose sprays of bright yellow, long-spurred flowers well above the foliage in mid-spring. Its clean evergreen foliage and vivid, clear yellow flower color make it a good choice for a shaded border or rock garden where year-round structure is valued alongside spring bloom. It spreads at a moderate, well-behaved pace by rhizome and is easy to grow under standard epimedium conditions, tolerating typical garden soil once established.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; twin-leaf epimedium is one of the smallest and daintiest species, best used at the front of a bed or in a trough where its delicate scale can be appreciated.

directions: Plant divisions in fall in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; twin-leaf epimedium is one of the smallest and daintiest species, best used at the front of a bed or in a trough where its delicate scale can be appreciated. Epimedium diphyllum is a diminutive Japanese species named for its distinctive leaves, which are divided into just two heart-shaped leaflets rather than the many leaflets typical of most epimedium, forming a low, tidy tuft topped with small, pure white, four-petaled flowers in spring. Its miniature scale and simple, elegant leaf structure make it a choice specialty plant for a shaded rock garden or the edge of a woodland path among other small treasures like dwarf hosta and Iris gracilipes. It spreads slowly and is easy to grow given consistent moisture and humus-rich soil, requiring little maintenance once established.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Delavay's mayapple is grown chiefly for its dramatically mottled foliage, which is most vivid in deeper shade with consistent moisture.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Delavay's mayapple is grown chiefly for its dramatically mottled foliage, which is most vivid in deeper shade with consistent moisture. Podophyllum delavayi is a striking Chinese woodland species grown primarily as a foliage plant, with deeply lobed, angular leaves marbled and mottled in bronze, silver-gray, and dark green patterns that rival the showiest hosta for foliage interest, along with small, drooping, deep maroon-red flowers hidden beneath the leaves in spring and red fruit in fall. Its intricately patterned leaves make it a prized textural accent for a shaded collector's border, container, or the front of a woodland planting where its foliage pattern can be appreciated at close range. Give it rich, evenly moist soil and shelter from harsh sun or wind, both of which can scorch the ornamental foliage.
